en: *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary*, Volume One, Part One.
Now, the True Dharma is empty and tranquil, its wondrousness transcending words and forms. Since words and forms are transcended, how could names and numerical categories be permitted within it?
Yet sentient beings dwell within the realm of seeing and hearing, remaining amidst the sphere of sight and sound.
Within this realm,
were it not for the manifestation of traces of his reflected image and the dissemination of the teachings of his spoken word, [this would not be possible].
There is no means to lead them back to the source,
nor to extend them into the transcendent;
therefore, the Great Sage Tathāgata—
Intending to manifest the true countenance in the Pure Land and extend a responsive form to the Sahā world,
he was thus able to descend his spirit to Tuṣita Heaven.
He was born in response to the royal palace;
he subdued Māra and attained the Way;
dwelling in the world, he bestowed his transformative teachings.
The traces of form and words have arisen from this point onward; however,
the faculties of sentient beings differ, being either sharp or dull.
Because the mind possesses the distinctions of breadth and narrowness,
it causes the single-flavored sacred scripture to manifest in immeasurable divisions;
though the teaching is thus divided into sections, [it remains one].
Broadly categorized, there are only two:
first, the Mahāyāna Dharma-gate of full syllables;
second, the Hīnayāna Dharma-gate of half-syllables.
Regarding the Mahāyāna method of full syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*):
from the time the Tathāgata first attained the Way until his final entry into *nirvāṇa*, [he taught it].
The followers of the Great Practice,
the various bodhisattvas and others,
expound the Avataṃsaka.
The ten stages,
the great cloud,
and the Dharma drum.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
the Mahāsannipāta,
and the Nirvāṇa [Sūtras].
In this way, throughout these immeasurable oceans of sūtras,
all such scriptures elucidate the two kinds of emptiness:
the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
The unconditioned Four Noble Truths are taught for those of great capacity,
so that they may advance toward the accomplishment of the Great Practice.
Because it is the ultimate among all vehicles for transporting beings, it is called the Mahāyāna Full-Syllable (Pūrṇākṣara).
It is termed "Full-Syllable" because its meaning is all-encompassing and complete.
The teaching of the minor vehicle’s half-syllables refers to that which the Tathāgata first intended at the Deer Park and continued until his final days at Śālavatī,
for the sake of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Those who follow the path of minor practices expound upon the Vinaya, the Abhidharma,
the Āgamas, and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka.
Such immeasurable sūtras of the Hīnayāna—
all these various scriptures merely clarify the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, there are those who preach the Four Noble Truths for the sake of those with limited capacities;
they advance toward the practice of the Lesser Vehicle,
yet their movement toward the welfare of beings has not reached its ultimate limit.
It is termed the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna);
its expression is narrow and its meaning is obscure,
thus it is called the "half-syllable."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Such suffering and so forth—
I [have taught] them in that Sūtra."
He ultimately did not explain it.
This present sutra, however, is subsumed within the full-syllable (pūrṇākṣara) teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Within these Mahāyāna full-syllable teachings, [it is as follows].
Throughout the Tathāgata’s entire career,
he preached the eight classes of Prajñāpāramitā,
benefiting beings of his time.
What are the eight?
The first section consists of one hundred thousand verses;
the second section consists of twenty-five thousand verses.
These two sections still exist in the Western lands,
but they are not found in this country.
The third part consists of eighteen thousand verses;
herein it is called the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
The fourth part consists of eight thousand verses.
Among these, the one called the *Prajñāpāramitā in Eight Thousand Lines* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā) is the fifth section,
consisting of four thousand verses;
the sixth section consists of two thousand five hundred verses.
These two sections exist in the Hu (Khotanese) original,
but have never before been translated.
The seventh section contains six hundred verses;
herein it is titled the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*.
The eighth section contains three hundred verses.
This is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Although there are eight numerical categories,
it receives only two names.
The first seven sections are all titled *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*;
the eighth section is titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
However, since the names are only two,
the reason there are eight sections is that the assemblies at different times were distinct.
There is a principle underlying the breadth and brevity [of these teachings]; thus, there is the enumeration of eight sections.
The first seven are *mahā*.
To manifest the great through the small,
one takes "Dharma" as the name;
this does not lack the meaning of "Vajra."
The eighth is the Vajra.
This is a metaphorical illustration of the Dharma,
manifesting its power to subdue afflictions.
It is not that the meaning of "maha" is absent;
rather, the names are established through mutual dependence.
Furthermore, there is the "King of Men."
The *Prasphullitapradīpa*,
the *Mahāśūnyatā*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated:
"These are all chapters from within the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred thousand verses;
they are not separate sections."
Among the eight great classes of beings,
there are none who do not exhaustively master the essential meanings of all scriptures and fully comprehend the ultimate principles of the myriad dharmas.
It clearly reveals the eternal fruit of Buddhahood,
the ultimate and perfect retribution,
and the Buddha-nature as the primary cause.
The ten stages are the revealing cause;
they consist of two kinds of wisdom:
the understanding that manifests the nature.
When the nature of fulfillment is revealed through understanding,
one realizes the eternal fruit within the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Its virtues are complete.
If one discusses its essence,
it has been pure throughout all time, from antiquity to the present.
Free from existence and free from non-existence;
the path of language is cut off,
and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
If one were to explain its function,
then the signless is never without signs;
its great functioning is without fixed direction.
It pervades the entire dharma-realm;
this is the great sovereign of the eight classes [of beings].
Now, as for the term "Vajra":
This is a name used by way of metaphor;
however, "vajra" in the world has many meanings.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* briefly clarifies three kinds [of gold]:
first, that which is the most refined among jewels,
rare and difficult to obtain.
If a person obtains it,
they will eliminate poverty and attain merit;
its two essential natures are firm and substantial.
It can destroy all things,
yet it cannot be used as a sacrificial offering by any thing.
The third is the Jewel that Abides According to Conditions.
It can ward off poisonous vapors;
the metaphor for prajñā is likewise.
This clarifies the sublime wisdom of prajñā.
The sovereign of all myriad practices;
if a person attains it,
they will leave behind the poverty of birth and death.
It realizes the fruit of the merit and bliss of nirvana.
Second, it clarifies prajñā-wisdom,
which takes this dharma-nature as its essence.
It can either fill or exhaust the source;
it is not subjected to the cutting up of afflictions.
It is similar in that the dwelling place of the threefold prajñā is not surrounded by malevolent demons.
Using this as a metaphor,
it is therefore called "Vajra Prajñā."
This is the pronunciation of the Central Kingdom's language;
here in this region it is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
It is able to illuminate the entirety of the void-source.
It thoroughly examines all phenomena;
therefore, it is called wisdom.
It nevertheless follows those vocal sounds.
The term "Prajñāpāramitā" is also a transliteration of a Western [Indic] sound.
This term is called "crossing over" (tīraṇa);
it is also said to mean "reaching the other shore.
It elucidates the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Cleansing and ascending through successive stages,
it is called the "other shore.
If a person practices and studies Prajñā, [they shall reach it].
Thus one can transcend birth and death and attain Great Nirvana,
preserving that vocal sound.
It is called a *pāramitā*.
As for "sūtra," in the Middle Kingdom it is called *sūtra*.
This method is called the "Root," which clarifies the speech of the sages and is able to [benefit] sentient beings.
Giving rise to the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome is the foundation of cultivating the Path; furthermore, when principle and teaching are viewed in relation to one another,
they mutually serve as each other's foundation.
Principles do not manifest themselves spontaneously;
they are revealed through teaching.
If one cannot express them in words, [they remain unmanifest].
There is no means by which realization can be attained.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"Although the fruit does not abide in the path..."
Yet the Way can serve as the cause;
this clarifies that the teaching is the foundation of the principle.
However, the teaching does not manifest of its own accord.
It arises by virtue of reasoning;
therefore, the treatise says:
"If one does not realize it..."
Thus, one would be unable to explain it.
This clarifies that principle is the foundation of the teaching;
it possesses these two meanings.
Therefore, it is called the "Root.
What is now referred to as "jīng" (sūtra) is actually the name for the "Five Classics" of this land.
The character for "beard" (鬚) should be used for *sūtra*;
it is not the banner of the true marks.
This is why the character for "scripture" (經) may be employed.
Regarding "resembling the beard," there are generally three meanings.
First, it refers to the similarity between people.
Second, the meaning of "constant" is the same [as in the previous case].
Third, it accords with what people value.
Because it possesses these meanings, [it is so designated].
I shall replace it with the Sūtras.
The Sūtras represent the eternal.
Thus, whether it be former sages or later saints, [they remain constant].
Metabolism varies,
yet the wind and ritual of the gentleman remain constant from beginning to end; therefore,
they are called "constant" (chang).
The illumination of the Buddha-dharma is likewise.
For although the Buddhas of the three periods of time pass away or remain according to circumstances, [the Dharma remains].
Because the instructional methods are eternally fixed,
they are called "Sūtras.
As for the "Śāstras," these were produced after the Buddha had passed away.
Within this series of images,
there is a Mahāyāna bodhisattva from Northern India named Vaśupāṇḍa.
He is also named Vasubandhu;
in this land [China], he is called the Bodhisattva of the Heavenly Court,
and is also known as the Bodhisattva Devaputra (Asaṅga’s brother).
In the *Dharmatrāta-piṭaka*,
he is the twentieth person;
he was truly a Great Being of sublime conduct.
His wondrous eloquence surpassed all others;
he had a comprehensive insight into the intended meaning of the Tathāgata’s teachings, both great and small.
He often observed that the text of this sutra was concise while its meaning was profound and hidden.
The principles and teachings are profound and subtle;
I fear that sentient beings of the final age,
upon seeking this brief text, [may fail to grasp their full meaning].
Having no means by which to attain awakening,
I have therefore looked up to the sacred scriptures and composed this treatise in its entirety.
He extensively expounded upon the true nature of reality and proclaimed its profound essentials,
desiring now to manifest the firm center and raise up once more the Great Way.
Thus, the lamp of the inexhaustible Dharma shines its brilliance through the long night;
herein lie the questions, answers, and explanations.
This is titled a "Renowned Treatise," and thus this scripture is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Now, when a Sage appears in the world...
This is solely for the benefit of sentient beings;
however, the paths to benefit are manifold,
and the gates of transformation are not one.
The transformative mental karma provides secret empowerment, augmenting mindfulness and increasing the Path.

Furthermore, there are three types of those capable of transformation: those who transform for the sake of sentient beings; [those who transform for their own benefit]; and [those who transform for both].
There are also three kinds:
first, false refuge;
second, ignorance of the Dharma.
Those in the third dhyāna are silent beings;
those who take refuge in the heterodox have the intention to seek liberation.
However, that upon which they rely is not correct;
therefore, it is called a false refuge.
For the sake of these sentient beings, the Tathāgata...
Therefore, by means of physical actions and supernormal powers,
he manifests the superior matters of the Buddha-dharma and transforms their deviant minds.
To turn them back and cause them to enter the correct path—
this is bodily action that benefits sentient beings who have taken refuge in what is false.
Regarding "one who does not yet know":
this person reveres and has faith in the Buddha and the Dharma,
but they have not yet understood the Dharma.
Therefore, by means of the eloquence of oral karma,
he extensively expounded the gateways of the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the methods for cultivating the path.
To cause them to understand:
this is the verbal karma for teaching and transforming sentient beings who do not yet know the Dharma.
As for the one who practices meditative silence:
such a person delights solely in solitude and tranquility,
and feels aversion toward clamor and distraction.
It is fitting that you should secretly assist through the karma of intention,
so as to cause them to advance in their stages on the Path;
this is the function of karma.
This benefits those who practice meditative silence.
These three types of persons are mentioned generally to illustrate the differences among the three karmas.
If we consider the beginning and end of a single person, there must also be the three types of karma.
Why is this so? Because this person—
Although there are those who seek the Way with resolve,
they do not yet know the method for attaining it;
therefore, he first demonstrates the supernormal powers of physical action.
This causes them to give rise to right faith; yet,
although they have attained right faith,
they still do not yet know the Dharma.
Next, by means of verbal action, one approaches the Dharma to cause them to attain understanding.
Although they may thus give rise to faith and achieve understanding, [the process continues].
Since one has not yet attained realization,
one employs mental action together with mindfulness to cause that realization to be attained.
Now, this sutra is, among the three types of karma,
the benefit of verbal karma for the sake of sentient beings who do not yet know the Dharma.
"Turning the Wheel of Dharma so that they may come to know"— from this point downward,
the entirety of the practice constitutes the general essence of this sutra.
If one follows the traditional interpretation of this region,
regardless of whether the text is extensive or concise,
it is all divided into three parts.
That is to say, the introduction, the main body,
and the dissemination; according to foreign Dharma masters, within this sutra:
It is divided into twelve sections:
first, the introductory section;
second, the section on protection and entrustment.
The third is the section on the stages of abiding;
the fourth is the section on practice according to reality;
and the fifth is the section on the Tathāgata’s non-conditioned characteristics.
The sixth is the section on faith;
the seventh is the section on comparative evaluation;
the eighth is the section on revealing the nature.
The ninth is the section on benefits;
the tenth is the section on severing doubts;
the eleventh is the section on the path of non-abiding.
The twelfth section is the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding dedication).
If categorized according to the three divisions,
this first part clarifies the introduction.
Furthermore, the supplementary sections in circulation constitute ten parts;
these are still the primary exposition.
However, regarding the twelve divisions [of the scriptures],
their names are explained and their origins are established,
which gives rise to a state of doubt.
This shall be explained when the time comes;
for now, I shall briefly arrange them according to their meaning so that the flow of the text remains connected.
Therefore, among the twelve divisions [of the scriptures],
the introduction (nidāna) is explained first;
for it is simply because the Tathāgata, throughout kalpas of vast antiquity...
Having accumulated merit and realized the Dharma within oneself,
one desires to explain and demonstrate what one has attained to sentient beings.
Yet sentient beings do not yet know that the Tathāgata has attained this inconceivable Dharma;
for this reason, he first provisionally relies upon time and location.
It initiates the capacities of all sentient beings;
by means of this, the subsequent correct exposition is brought forth.
Therefore, it is the first.
I have separately clarified its sequence;
the meaning of the introduction is already manifest.
It would be appropriate to proceed with the discourse immediately; however, the Dharma must be requested by someone.
If one were to preach without being requested,
those who hear the Dharma would not give rise to the perception that it is difficult to encounter.
Therefore, Subhūti, before making his formal request, first offers praise.
He praises the Tathāgata for being well able to protect, mindfully attend to, and entrust [the teaching] to two kinds of bodhisattvas; thus, he names this section after that praise.
Therefore, secondly, the section on protection,
mindfulness, and entrustment follows,
which is praised prior to this.
Even though he requested the rules for dwelling in a place, the Tathāgata, in response to that request,
explained at length the methods and applications for dwelling;
therefore, this is the third [chapter].
Next, the section on abiding is explained.
Although one’s virtuous qualities may be fully perfected while abiding,
it is appropriate to practice further advancement.
If one does not further cultivate the myriad practices,
the path to the fruit of Buddhahood will be remote,
and there will be no means to realize it swiftly.
Therefore, fourth, next is the section clarifying the practice of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*).
Now that the superior practices have been accomplished.
Thus, through the path, one becomes fully perfected;
yet because one does not bestow [merit] falsely,
the principle brings forth a superior retribution.
The cause is established through signlessness,
and the unconditioned fruit is realized.
Therefore, this is the fifth.
Next, the section clarifying that the Tathāgata does not possess conditioned characteristics is explained.
For the cause is profound and the fruit is wondrous;
thus, the Sage’s discernment is not in vain.
The sixth section, on those with faith:
since this has been taught according to the specific capacity of the audience,
there will certainly be those who believe in and accept this profound sutra.
The merit therein is even greater.
Were it not for the comparison with a proximate analogy,
there would be no way to manifest the vastness of the merit of upholding this sutra.
Therefore, the seventh section follows by clarifying the comparative analysis of its superior merit; specifically,
the merit obtained from upholding this sutra.
Thus, one is able to foster and give rise to wondrous understanding,
manifesting the fundamental reality of non-attainment as already realized for one's own use;
therefore, this is the eighth stage.
Next is the section on the manifestation of nature.
Now that the principle of nature has been manifested,
the wisdom-observation becomes increasingly clear.
This enables the practitioner to closely eliminate karmic obstacles and shall cause them to attain the wondrous fruit.
From the time before he attained Buddhahood until now,
there is no superior reward among humans or devas that he has not fully experienced.
Therefore, the ninth section clarifies the benefits.
Now, how could the near-term rewards of humans and devas possibly lead to the great fruit of Bodhi? [They do so because...]
It may indeed be attained immediately; yet,
were it not for the complete severing of all doubts,
there would be no means by which it could be verified.
Therefore, tenth, next follows the section clarifying the severance of doubt;
now that the net of doubt has been eliminated.
Thus, one is able to discern and eliminate birth and death;
therefore, while dwelling together with the world,
one is further able to possess great compassion.
Agitating the three realms of existence and not abiding in nirvana,
it next clarifies the eleventh section: the Stage of the Non-abiding Path.
However, all that has been explained above was for the benefit of those present at that time;
yet, out of great compassion, the Tathāgata further desires to use this supreme Dharma.
Its grace moistens distant generations.
Therefore, the twelfth section follows to clarify the section on circulation (pariṇāmanā).
First, the introduction is clarified.
Regarding the term "introduction" (nidāna):
it refers to the exposition of the preceding causes and conditions.
The introduction to what is being explained is termed the "preface.
There are two kinds of prefaces.
First is the testimony of faith;
second is the introduction to the origin [of the teaching].
Regarding the testimony of faith:
The name is derived from its function;
as for the "Introductory Section on Origination," it is named after its essential nature.
Within the two introductory sections,
there are three clarifications.
The first explains the intent behind establishing the two introductions.
Second, the two explanations of the two prefaces involve inclusion and exclusion.
Third, the judgment regarding the scope—general or specific—of the textual passages of the two prefaces.
First, the meaning of the preface is clarified.
Generally speaking, when one speaks of a "preface," it serves as a preface to a sutra;
since the sutra itself is non-dual, [the preface is likewise so].
For what reason is there a dual introduction?
The explanation says:
if the sutra were only one.
The prologues themselves do not differ;
however, since what is now a single scripture has become two scriptures,
it is necessary to establish two prologues.
Why is it that one sūtra becomes two?
It is because the Dharma issues from the Buddha’s own mouth;
thus, these are sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
It was transmitted to Ānanda.
These are the sūtras transmitted by Ānanda;
specifically, those texts transmitted by Ānanda that were inscribed upon bamboo slips and silk.
It benefits the future as spoken by the Tathāgata;
it benefits the present.
This is precisely because there are differences in the lineages of high and low among people,
and there is a distinction between the two periods of the present and the future;
for this reason.
One sūtra becomes two;
for these two sūtras,
two introductory sections must be established.
Regarding the present Tathāgata,
one must establish the introductory narrative;
regarding the future Ānanda’s transmission, [one must establish the lineage].
One must establish the *nidāna* (序) for the purpose of providing proof and inspiration.
Second, in distinguishing the names of the two *nidānas*, there are instances of inclusion and exclusion;
however, the general meaning of these two *nidānas* is as follows.
All are for the purpose of engendering faith;
if one lacks the vessel of faith,
the Dharma will not be transmitted.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata is about to preach the Dharma,
he first manifests auspicious signs.
One generates pure faith;
by means of this generation,
one causes sentient beings to give rise to faith.
This is the sequence of testimony and faith (*saddhādeśanā*).
However, that which Ānanda cited was intended to initiate the transmission.
This is also the introduction for the commencement [of the teaching].
If that is so, both introductions apply;
with what intention, then, did Ānanda place [the introduction] at the beginning of the sutra?
This is called the "Preface of Certification and Faith.
At the beginning of the Tathāgata’s sūtras,
the "Preface of the Arousing [of the Teaching]" is established.
The commentary states: The Buddha is a Great Sage;
it is logically appropriate that he be trusted.
Therefore, the title is derived from the introductory section.
This is called the "Introductory Chapter on the Arousing [of Resolve].
Ānanda is an insufficient person;
I fear that those in the future will not believe.
Therefore, it is named according to the matter of "testimony and faith" (saddhā-deśanā);
thus, it is called the "Testimony and Faith Introduction.
Thirdly, the explanation of the two introductions.
The sequence of the sūtra text is reversed;
the two phrases "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) are positioned at the beginning in relation to the sūtras of the present Tathāgata.
It is entirely without origination;
with respect to the *Ānanda-sūtra* of the future,
it is entirely a matter of verified faith.
From "At one time" onwards,
all [the sections] have the meaning of looking toward the Tathāgata as being present.
How is this known?
It is because the time, the place,
and the eight [factors] are essential for the arising of discourse.
Thus, one knows that there was an instigation.
At that time, the World-Honored One descended;
Ānanda then led [the person] forward.
This also establishes the meaning of the proof;
however, only the first six phrases of the sutra constitute the Buddha’s instruction to Ānanda.
It is placed at the beginning of all sutras;
therefore, it is judged to be the "Sincerity and Faith Introduction" (saddharmapuṇḍarīka-nidāna).
From the words "At that time, the World-Honored One," and so forth...
This clarifies that the specific events of the initiation differ from those in other sūtras; therefore,
it is judged to be the "Initiation Introduction" (nidāna).
Within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the section on the testimony of faith (*saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śraddhā-varga*), there are six phrases,
the first being "Thus" (*evam*).
2. Thus have I heard;
3. at one time;
4. the Bhagavān; 5. the dwelling place.
Sixth is "hearing together.
However, the general purport of these six points is entirely to engender faith.
It also serves the purpose of distinguishing [this teaching] from the *āda* (primordial matter) and other such concepts held by non-Buddhists, thereby providing evidence for the arising of faith.
This is why "thus" (*evam*) is first indicated;
for if the essence of the Dharma were not first established at the outset, [the subsequent discourse would lack a foundation].
Thus, faith would have no basis to rely upon.
For this reason, [the text] first clarifies "Thus have I heard."
This gives rise to those capable of hearing.
Since the Dharma is placed at the beginning,
there must necessarily be people who hear it.
Therefore, next, "I heard" is explained.
As for "at one time," this clarifies the temporal occasion of hearing the sutra.
Since there are persons capable of hearing,
there must necessarily be a time for hearing;
therefore, "at one time" is explained next.
"Bhagavān" refers to the person capable of teaching;
the objection states that hearing [the teaching] occurs at a specific time.
Since it was not known from whom this was heard,
the Buddha Bhagavat is explained next,
even though he is the one who discerns and teaches.
However, a teaching must necessarily have its locus;
therefore, it next states:
"In the city of Śrāvastī."
Although the location was known,
it was still not known with whom he had heard [the teaching];
therefore, it next says "with a great assembly of bhikṣus."
Together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people,
the words and their meanings mutually reinforce one another,
all serving to establish faith.
"Thus" is a term signifying faith and compliance. Now,
the Great Ocean of the Buddha-dharma—
One enters by means of faith and crosses over by means of wisdom. Regarding faith,
it should be said as follows:
This matter is thus.
One who does not believe should say:
"This matter is not thus."
A person endowed with faith who enters into the Buddha-dharma brings about great benefit.
Therefore, at the very beginning of the Buddha-dharma,
it is first proclaimed in this way,
even before the signs of faith have yet arisen.
The commentary explains this in detail;
here, I have merely explained the general meaning and have not yet analyzed the wording.
Now, for one who has such faith,
there are two kinds of understanding.
The first pertains to the Buddha.
Second, regarding the principle.
As for the understanding of the Buddhas,
this clarifies the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
What is taught is not different [from reality];
therefore it is called "Tathā" (Thusness).
Because it is taught in accordance [with reality].
It is so named because it is precisely what all Buddhas have taught in common;
therefore, it is trustworthy.
Regarding "conforming to principle":
this clarifies that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena remains unchanged throughout past and present.
Therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā).
Because it is spoken as such,
it is named "this."
Since these are words that accord with reality,
being neither more nor less than the truth,
they are certainly trustworthy.
Therefore, it is said "thus.
Regarding "I have heard":
next, the person who hears is explained.
One should ask: "Who is this that is called 'I'?
Furthermore, in the Buddha-dharma there is no self;
for what reason, then, do you refer to it as "I"?
Furthermore, it should properly be "heard by the ear.
Why, then, is it said "I heard"?
